module_title: Core DJ Skills and Mixing Techniques

lessons.title: Beatmatching and Tempo Adjustment
lessons.body: Beatmatching is the foundation of DJing. It means aligning two tracks so their beats hit at exactly the same time, creating a seamless blend. Start with two copies of the same song. On your controller or CDJs, set the pitch fader to 0%. Play track A, then press play on track B on the first beat of a bar. You'll hear a 'train wreck' if they're off. Use the jog wheel to nudge track B forward or backward until the kicks lock. In Africa, where many genres like Afrobeats, Amapiano, and Kuduro have tempos between 100-120 BPM, you'll often adjust by 2-4%. For example, if track A is 110 BPM and track B is 112 BPM, slow B down by about 1.8%. Count beats aloud: '1-2-3-4'. If track B drifts ahead, gently touch the jog wheel's edge to slow it. If it lags, push it forward. Practice 15 minutes daily with a metronome app like Soundbrenner. Once you can match two identical tracks, try different songs from the same genre. Remember, your ears are the final judge, not the BPM display. In loud African parties, use headphones with good isolation, like Audio-Technica ATH-M50x, to hear the cue mix clearly.

lessons.title: Phrasing and Harmonic Mixing
lessons.body: Phrasing means mixing at the right moment in a song's structure. Most African dance tracks follow a 8-bar or 16-bar phrase pattern. For instance, an Amapiano song might have an 8-bar intro, then a 16-bar main section. Count bars: 1-2-3-4 (one bar), repeat 8 times. Mix in during the last 8 bars of a phrase, so the new track's first downbeat lands on the next phrase start. Harmonic mixing uses musical keys to avoid clashes. Use the Camelot Wheel: tracks with the same number (e.g., 8A and 8B) or adjacent numbers (8A to 9A) mix smoothly. For example, if track A is in 8A (A minor), track B in 8B (C major) works because they share notes. Free tools like Mixed In Key or Rekordbox analyze keys. In Africa, many producers label keys on Beatport or local platforms like Afrodesia. Practice by mixing two tracks in the same key, then move one step around the wheel. Always trust your ears: if it sounds sour, don't force it. Harmonic mixing keeps the energy flowing, especially during long sets at weddings or clubs in Lagos or Nairobi.

lessons.title: Using Effects and Filters Creatively
lessons.body: Effects and filters add energy, tension, and surprise. Start with a low-pass filter (LPF) on your mixer. Turn it down to cut highs, creating a muffled sound, then slowly open it on a build-up. For example, during a 16-bar build in an Afro-house track, close the LPF at bar 8, then open it fully at bar 16 for a drop. Use a high-pass filter (HPF) to remove bass before a breakdown, then bring it back. Echo effects work well on vocal stabs: set echo to 1/4 beat, feedback 50%, and tap it on the last word of a phrase. Reverb adds spaceâuse 20% wet on a snare hit. In African genres, delay is popular on talking drum samples. Don't overdo it: too many effects muddy the mix. Practice with a single effect per transition. On Pioneer DJM mixers, the Color FX knob is your friend. For beginners, the 'Filter' knob on a DDJ-400 is easy to reach. Record your practice and listen backâif the effect distracts from the groove, reduce it.

lessons.title: Live Remixing and Mashups
lessons.body: Live remixing means combining parts of multiple tracks on the fly. A mashup layers an acapella from one song over the instrumental of another. For example, take the vocals from 'Fall' by Davido (105 BPM) and the beat from 'Ye' by Burna Boy (105 BPM). They share tempo, so beatmatch first. Use a 4-bar loop on the instrumental to keep it steady. Then bring in the acapella on the first beat of a phrase. Adjust the acapella's key with a pitch shifter if neededâmost DJ software like Serato or Virtual DJ has key lock. For a live remix, use hot cues to jump between sections: cue 1 for intro, cue 2 for chorus. In African parties, mashups of Afrobeats with Amapiano are crowd-pleasers. Try blending 'Essence' by Wizkid with a log drum loop from an Amapiano track. Practice by recording your mashups and sharing on WhatsApp groups for feedback. Keep volumes balanced: acapella at 0 dB, instrumental at -3 dB. Always have a backup planâif it clashes, cut the acapella and let the beat play.

lessons.title: Scratching and Turntablism Basics
lessons.body: Scratching is moving a record or jog wheel back and forth while the crossfader cuts the sound. Start with a 'baby scratch': set the crossfader to the channel with the scratch sound (e.g., a vocal 'ahh' or drum hit). Move the record forward and back in one smooth motion, without moving the crossfader. Practice 10 minutes daily. Next, add the crossfader: cut the sound off when pulling back, open when pushing forward. This is a 'chirp scratch'. For African DJs, scratching over Amapiano log drums or Afrobeat horn stabs works well. Use a scratch sample from your software or a real vinyl. Set your mixer's crossfader curve to sharp (not smooth) for clean cuts. On controllers, the jog wheel tension can be adjustedâtighten it for better control. Learn the 'transformer scratch': click the crossfader on and off rapidly while moving the record. Don't overuse scratches; one well-timed scratch per 8 bars is enough. Record yourself and listen for timing. Turntablism is a skill that takes months, so be patient.

lessons.title: Reading the Crowd and Adapting Your Mix
lessons.body: Reading the crowd means watching and listening to know what they want. At an African wedding, start with highlife or old-school R&B during dinner, then move to Afrobeats when dancing begins. Look for feet tapping, heads nodding, or people leaving the floor. If the floor empties, change the genre or tempo within 30 seconds. Use a 'peak-time' track like 'Ojuelegba' by Wizkid to bring energy back. In clubs, keep an eye on the barâif people buy drinks, they're happy. Adjust your mix: if the crowd is older, play more 90s Kwaito or Congolese rumba. If young, go for Amapiano or Afrobeats. Have a 'reset' track readyâa familiar hit that always works. Talk to the MC or event planner for cues. In Lagos or Accra, crowds respond to call-and-response; drop a track with a chant. Always have a backup playlist on a USB or phone in case your laptop fails. Adapt volume too: louder for peak, softer for chill. Record your sets and note which tracks got the biggest reaction.

quiz.q: What is the primary goal of beatmatching?
options: A) To align two tracks so their beats hit at the same time
B) To change the key of a track
C) To add effects to a mix
D) To scratch over a beat
quiz.explanation: Beatmatching synchronizes the timing of two tracks for a seamless blend.

quiz.q: If track A is 110 BPM and track B is 112 BPM, how much should you adjust track B's pitch to match?
options: B) Slow it down by about 1.8%
quiz.explanation: To match 110 BPM, track B at 112 BPM must be slowed by approximately 1.8%.

quiz.q: Which tool is recommended for hearing the cue mix clearly in loud African parties?
options: C) Headphones with good isolation like Audio-Technica ATH-M50x
quiz.explanation: Isolating headphones block outside noise, letting you hear the cue mix accurately.

quiz.q: What is phrasing in DJing?
options: A) Mixing at the right moment in a song's structure
quiz.explanation: Phrasing means aligning mixes with the song's bar and phrase patterns.

quiz.q: How many bars are typically in a phrase in African dance tracks?
quiz.explanation: Most African dance tracks follow 8-bar or 16-bar phrase structures.

quiz.q: What does the Camelot Wheel help with?
quiz.explanation: The Camelot Wheel shows compatible musical keys for harmonic mixing.

quiz.q: If track A is in 8A, which track key would mix smoothly?
quiz.explanation: 8B is the relative major of 8A and shares notes, making it compatible.

quiz.q: Which free tool can analyze musical keys?
quiz.explanation: Mixed In Key, Rekordbox, and Serato all offer key analysis features.

quiz.q: What does a low-pass filter do?
options: A) Cuts highs, creating a muffled sound
B) Cuts lows, making it thin
quiz.explanation: A low-pass filter allows low frequencies and attenuates highs.

quiz.q: When using an echo effect on a vocal stab, what settings are suggested?
quiz.explanation: A 1/4 beat echo with 50% feedback creates a rhythmic repeat without muddiness.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for using effects in a mix?
options: A) Use as many as possible
B) Use one effect per transition
quiz.explanation: Using one effect per transition keeps the mix clean and focused.

quiz.q: What does a high-pass filter do?
options: A) Removes bass before a breakdown
quiz.explanation: A high-pass filter cuts low frequencies, useful for removing bass.

quiz.q: What is a mashup?
options: A) Layering an acapella over an instrumental
quiz.explanation: A mashup combines vocals from one track with the instrumental of another.

quiz.q: Which two songs are given as an example for a mashup?
options: A) 'Fall' by Davido and 'Ye' by Burna Boy
B) 'Essence' by Wizkid and 'Ojuelegba' by Wizkid
quiz.explanation: Both 'Fall' and 'Ye' are at 105 BPM, making them suitable for a mashup.

quiz.q: What is a hot cue used for in live remixing?
quiz.explanation: Hot cues let you quickly jump to specific points in a track.

quiz.q: What volume balance is suggested for a mashup?
options: A) Acapella at 0 dB, instrumental at -3 dB
C) Acapella at -3 dB, instrumental at 0 dB
quiz.explanation: Keeping the acapella slightly louder ensures vocals are clear.

quiz.q: What is a baby scratch?
options: A) Moving the record forward and back without moving the crossfader
C) Scratching with a baby sample
quiz.explanation: The baby scratch is the basic scratch without crossfader movement.

quiz.q: What is a chirp scratch?
options: A) Adding crossfader cuts to the baby scratch
B) Scratching with a chirp sound
C) A scratch using only the crossfader
quiz.explanation: The chirp scratch involves cutting the sound with the crossfader while moving the record.

quiz.q: What crossfader curve is recommended for scratching?
quiz.explanation: A sharp curve gives clean cuts for scratching.

quiz.q: How often should you scratch in a mix?
options: B) One well-timed scratch per 8 bars
quiz.explanation: Overusing scratches can distract; one per 8 bars is effective.

quiz.q: What is reading the crowd?
options: A) Watching and listening to know what they want
quiz.explanation: Reading the crowd means observing reactions to adjust your mix.

quiz.q: At an African wedding, what genre is suggested for dinner?
quiz.explanation: Highlife or old-school R&B suits the dinner atmosphere before dancing.

quiz.q: If the dance floor empties, how quickly should you change the music?
quiz.explanation: Quick changes keep the energy and prevent the floor from staying empty.

quiz.q: What track is suggested as a peak-time energy booster?
quiz.explanation: 'Ojuelegba' is a familiar hit that can revive the crowd.

quiz.q: What should you always have as a backup?
options: A) A playlist on USB or phone
quiz.explanation: A backup playlist ensures you can continue if your main device fails.

quiz.q: What is a 'reset' track?
options: A) A familiar hit that always works
B) A track that clears the floor
C) A track with no beat
quiz.explanation: A reset track is a reliable song that can bring the crowd back.

quiz.q: What should you do if a mashup clashes?
options: A) Cut the acapella and let the beat play
quiz.explanation: Removing the clashing element quickly restores a clean mix.

quiz.q: Which effect is popular on talking drum samples in African genres?
quiz.explanation: Delay adds rhythmic repeats that complement talking drum patterns.

quiz.q: What is the recommended daily practice time for beatmatching?
quiz.explanation: 15 minutes of focused daily practice builds beatmatching skills efficiently.

quiz.q: What is the first step in live remixing?
quiz.explanation: Beatmatching ensures the tracks are synchronized before layering.
